verses.1: Al-Mizan presents Noah as sent to warn his people before painful punishment overtakes them.
verses.2: Noah identifies himself as a manifest warner to his people.
verses.3: Al-Mizan presents Noah’s call: worship God, be wary of Him, and obey him, so that they may receive forgiveness and respite to a specified end which cannot be deferred when God’s end comes.
verses.4: Al-Mizan presents Noah’s call: worship God, be wary of Him, and obey him, so that they may receive forgiveness and respite to a specified end which cannot be deferred when God’s end comes.
verses.5: Al-Mizan reports Noah’s unceasing call, which only increased his people’s evasion.
verses.6: Al-Mizan reports Noah’s unceasing call, which only increased his people’s evasion.
verses.7: Al-Mizan depicts Noah’s people refusing his call to forgiveness: they shut out his message, persisted, and became arrogantly proud.
verses.8: Al-Mizan reports that Noah addressed his people loudly, publicly and privately, urging them to seek forgiveness from their All-Forgiving Lord.
verses.9: Al-Mizan reports that Noah addressed his people loudly, publicly and privately, urging them to seek forgiveness from their All-Forgiving Lord.
verses.10:
Al-Mizan says that the intensive Ghaffār establishes both the abundance and the unceasing continuity of divine forgiveness, which justifies Noah’s command to seek it. Samāʾ here means the clouds, midrār abundant pouring rain, and the apocopated yursil makes it the consequence of that command. Imdād is supply with what meets needs; wealth and children are primary human means, while gardens and streams are separately named important forms of wealth.

The commentary consequently holds that forgiveness affects the removal of widespread disasters and the opening of heavenly and earthly bounty. Natural conditions affect human ease and hardship, but are themselves tied to a society’s virtuous or vicious condition, as also indicated in (30:41), (42:30), and (7:96).

It retains rajāʾ in its original sense of hope, opposite to fear, rather than proposed senses of belief or fear: their failure to hope in God describes despair of receiving good from Him. While waqār is also glossed as greatness, Al-Mizan ultimately takes it in its root sense of stability, fixity, and establishment in divine lordship. Noah’s people despaired that God could fill the role of an established lord and therefore resorted to angels, jinn, and other beings as managers and intercessors, treating God only as originator beyond direct worship.

Al-Mizan answers that directing affairs is the successive creation of the constituents of the universal order. Since God creates everything, He is its Owner and Director, the sole Lord and sole object of worship. Direct worship is possible through His knowable attributes of action—the Creator, Sustainer, and Merciful—even though His essence cannot be comprehended.
verses.11: Al-Mizan promises that repentance will bring abundant rain, wealth, children, gardens, and streams.
verses.12: Al-Mizan promises that repentance will bring abundant rain, wealth, children, gardens, and streams.
verses.13: Al-Mizan asks why they deny God’s weight as Lord despite His creating them in successive stages.
verses.14:
Al-Mizan defines aṭwār as degrees, states, or positions and reads successive human development—from dust, sperm, clot, and lump of flesh through fetal and later life stages—as evidence of tadbīr, God’s direction and regulation of affairs. The diversity of the species in sex, colour, form, and capacity supplies the same proof: the Director of their affairs is their Lord and must be worshipped.

For the seven heavens, the commentary gives two possibilities for ṭibāq: they are one above another, or they resemble one another. ‘Seeing’ means knowing, and Noah’s use of this accepted belief in argument indicates that seven heavens belonged to the teachings of divine messengers before him.
verses.15: Al-Mizan invokes the seven layered heavens, moonlight, and the sun as a lamp.
verses.16:
Al-Mizan places the moon and sun within the proof that God is to be worshipped because His beneficent direction of affairs establishes His lordship. The sun is a lamp because it illuminates the world from itself; the moon is a light because it illuminates earth with light derived from the sun. Fīhinna refers collectively to the seven heavens as their encompassing space, though the moon is actually in only one of them.

The commentary takes humanity’s growth from earth literally: its root lies in mineral elements composed to absorb nourishment, grow, and reproduce, which is vegetative growth. Returning to earth is death and burial, and the new bringing forth is Resurrection for requital. Thumma makes the return a new stage, while the wāw joins return and resurrection as one process in which return is the prelude to emerging; both belong to the abode of reality, unlike this illusory world. The earth’s being a carpet means that it is made convenient for movement and travel.
verses.17: God made humankind grow from the earth as plants.
verses.18: God returns people to earth and brings them forth anew.
verses.19: Al-Mizan says God made the earth traversable through its spacious ways.
verses.20: Al-Mizan defines subul as paths and fijāj as broad roads, possibly paths between mountains. It then reads Noah as returning to his initial complaint after reporting every mode of his mission: affluent leaders induced the people to oppose him. Wealth and children, earlier named as blessings, increased their kufr rather than gratitude and therefore brought loss of divine mercy.
verses.21: Al-Mizan reports Noah’s complaint that his people followed the affluent, whose wealth and children increased only their loss, and plotted greatly.
verses.22:
Al-Mizan notes that kubbār intensifies kabīr. The elite commanded continued worship of all their idols and then singled out Wadd, Suwāʿ, Yaghūth, Yaʿūq, and Nasr, showing special regard for them; the absence of lā before the last two perhaps indicates that the first three were more important—God knows best.

The commentary takes ‘they led many astray’ as the leaders, consistently with the preceding plural pronouns, not the idols as some exegetes suggest. Noah’s prayer that the wrongdoers increase only in ḍalāl does not ask God to initiate their misguidance; it asks punishment after their own disbelief and wrongdoing. It is therefore distinct from his later prayer for their extermination.
verses.23:
Al-Mizan identifies the sūrah as Meccan and as a concise account of Noah’s mission, his people’s rejection, his complaint and curse, his prayer for believers, and their drowning. Noah’s warning means that punishment for their polytheism and sins was imminent and inevitable unless they took heed; the particle an explains the revealed mission.

Calling them ‘my people’ conveys Noah’s compassion and common bond. His threefold summons is to exclusive worship of God rather than idols treated as interceding lesser lords, to taqwá—refraining from every major and minor sin and performing obligatory good deeds—and to obey him as God’s messenger and teacher. Al-Mizan relates these respectively to monotheism, the hereafter that undergirds taqwá, and prophethood.

The promise to forgive ‘some’ sins concerns their past sins before conversion, including polytheism, not sins not yet committed or a licence for future wrongdoing. The commentary rejects the claim that Islam forgives all sins whereas prior religions forgive only some: the apparent general forgiveness in (61:10-12) rests on continuing faith and action, while (8:38) speaks of past sins even for those converting to Islam. It also rejects readings that make min redundant, merely explanatory, or a marker of starting point.

Al-Mizan distinguishes a specified ajal from another, unspecified end. Faithful response postpones death to the specified, longest assigned term; persistence in disbelief brings the other term sooner. God’s end means whatever He decrees and enacts, whether either kind of term, and cannot be postponed. It rejects restricting that end to one of the two, or making the specified term Resurrection, because this conflicts with the promised forgiveness. The concluding condition calls them to know this and obey; it reports, without adopting, readings that make it a general commendation of knowledge.

Noah’s ‘night and day’ denotes tireless, continuous preaching, while their firār is metaphorical evasion. The commentary explains that good placed in an unsuitable setting is met by its evil, as the Qur’an is mercy to believers yet increases wrongdoers in loss (17:82). His reference to forgiveness shows sincere concern for their good; fingers in ears and cloaks over faces figuratively portray deliberate refusal even to hear or see him, followed by obstinate, extreme pride. Thumma in his later report need not mark chronology: he called loudly and used both public proclamation and private conversation, trying every avenue.

verses.25: Al-Mizan says their sins led to drowning and fire, with no helper besides Allah.
verses.26: Al-Mizan records Noah’s prayer that no disbelieving inhabitant remain on earth.
verses.27: Al-Mizan says they would mislead God’s servants and beget only wholly disbelieving degenerates.
verses.28: Al-Mizan presents these verses as Noah’s people’s extermination and his final curse. Their sins caused their drowning in the storm, followed immediately by God’s admission of them to a punishing fire. The contrast of water and fire establishes barzakh, the intermediate realm where sinners are punished between death and resurrection; the commentary rejects taking the fire as merely the later Ākhirah, since fāʾ indicates immediate sequence. Their lack of helpers means that their idols and gods could not save them. Noah’s request that no dayyār, an inhabitant, of the disbelievers be left on earth completes his curse; the drowning verse is a parenthesis confirming that it was answered and that they were completely eradicated. Divine revelation told him that their survival would benefit neither believers, whom they would mislead, nor their descendants, whom they would only beget as intensely disbelieving and impious. He then seeks forgiveness for himself, his parents, the believers of his people whom “whoever enters my house” denotes, and faithful men and women until the Resurrection. Tabār means destruction and apparently includes worldly drowning together with what leads to otherworldly punishment; this is Noah’s last Qurʾānic speech.
